source.title: Statements and open problems on decidable sets X ⊆ N that contain informal notions and refer to the current knowledge on X

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a decidable set X ⊆ N such that all five of the paper's Conditions (1)–(5) hold simultaneously? Here Condition (1) says that a known algorithm with no input returns an integer n such that, if X is finite, then every element of X is at most n. Condition (2) says that there is a known algorithm deciding, for every k ∈ N, whether k ∈ X. Condition (3) says that no known algorithm with no input returns the truth value of the statement that X is infinite. Condition (4) says that X has many known elements and it is conjectured, but not yet proved, that X is infinite. Condition (5) says that X is naturally defined, the infiniteness of X is false or unproven, and among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same known elements, X has the simplest definition.
accepted.context_brief: Existence of a set meeting Conditions (1)–(5)

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1. Is there a set X ⊆ N which satisfies Conditions (1)-(5)?

Definition 1.2. Conditions (1)-(5) concern sets X ⊆ N.
(1) A known algorithm with no input returns an integer n satisfying card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].
(2) A known algorithm for every k ∈ N decides whether or not k ∈ X.
(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the logical value of the statement card(X) = ω.
(4) There are many elements of X and it is conjectured, though so far unproven, that X is infinite.
(5) X is naturally defined. The infiniteness is false or unproven. X has the simplest definition among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same set of known elements.

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many primes of the form k! + 1, where k! denotes the factorial of the positive integer k?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.1. ([1, p. 443], [5]). The are infinitely many primes of the form k! + 1.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a decidable set X ⊆ N such that Condition (1), Condition (2), Condition (4), and Condition (5) all hold, but Condition (3) fails? Equivalently, is there such an X for which a known algorithm with no input does return the truth value of the statement that X is infinite, while there is still a known threshold integer for X if X is finite, membership in X is decidable for every natural number, X has many known elements and is conjectured to be infinite, and X is naturally defined in the sense of Definition 1.2?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 2. Is there a set X ⊆ N that satisfies the conjunction
(Condition 1) ∧ (Condition 2) ∧ ¬(Condition 3) ∧ (Condition 4) ∧ (Condition 5)?

Definition 1.2. Conditions (1)-(5) concern sets X ⊆ N.
(1) A known algorithm with no input returns an integer n satisfying card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].
(2) A known algorithm for every k ∈ N decides whether or not k ∈ X.
(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the logical value of the statement card(X) = ω.
(4) There are many elements of X and it is conjectured, though so far unproven, that X is infinite.
(5) X is naturally defined. The infiniteness is false or unproven. X has the simplest definition among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same set of known elements.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a decidable set X ⊆ N such that Condition (2), Condition (4), and Condition (5) hold, but both Condition (1) and Condition (3) fail? That is, can one find a naturally defined set X with decidable membership and many known elements, conjectured but not proved to be infinite, for which there is no known threshold integer of the type in Condition (1), and for which a known algorithm with no input does return the truth value of the statement that X is infinite?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 3. Is there a set X ⊆ N that satisfies the conjunction
¬(Condition 1) ∧ (Condition 2) ∧ ¬(Condition 3) ∧ (Condition 4) ∧ (Condition 5)?

Definition 1.2. Conditions (1)-(5) concern sets X ⊆ N.
(1) A known algorithm with no input returns an integer n satisfying card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].
(2) A known algorithm for every k ∈ N decides whether or not k ∈ X.
(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the logical value of the statement card(X) = ω.
(4) There are many elements of X and it is conjectured, though so far unproven, that X is infinite.
(5) X is naturally defined. The infiniteness is false or unproven. X has the simplest definition among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same set of known elements.

accepted.question_text: Is there a known threshold number for the set P_{n^2+1} of primes of the form n^2 + 1? In the paper's terminology, this asks whether there exists a known integer n such that, if P_{n^2+1} is finite, then every prime of the form m^2 + 1 belongs to (−∞, n].
accepted.context_brief: Threshold number for primes of the form n^2 + 1

evidence.quote: Open Problem 4. Is there a known threshold number of Pn^2+1?

Definition 3.3. We say that an integer n is a threshold number of a set X ⊆ N, if
card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].

Edmund Landau’s conjecture states that the set Pn^2+1 of primes of the form n^2 + 1 is
infinite, see [13], [14], [16].

accepted.question_text: Is there a known threshold number for the set T of twin primes? In the paper's terminology, this asks whether there exists a known integer n such that, if the set of twin primes is finite, then every twin prime is at most n.

evidence.quote:
Let T denote the set of twin primes.
Open Problem 5. Is there a known threshold number of T?

Definition 3.3. We say that an integer n is a threshold number of a set X ⊆ N, if
card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many prime Fermat numbers, that is, infinitely many primes of the form 2^(2^k) + 1 with k ∈ N?

evidence.quote: It is open whether or not there are infinitely many primes of the form 2^(2^k) + 1, see [7, p. 158] and [11, p. 74].

accepted.question_text: Are there infinitely many composite Fermat numbers, that is, infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^k) + 1 with k ∈ N?

evidence.quote: It is open whether or not there are infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^k) + 1, see [7, p. 159] and [11, p. 74].

needs_review.question_text_raw: Statement 1. The statement ∃n ∈ N (card(Pn^2+1) < ω ⇒ Pn^2+1 ⊆ [2, n + 3]) remains unproven in ZFC and classical logic without the law of excluded middle.

evidence.quote:
Statement 1. The statement
∃n ∈ N (card(Pn^2+1) < ω ⇒ Pn^2+1 ⊆ [2, n + 3])
remains unproven in ZFC and classical logic without the law of excluded middle.
